title: Epsilon-NFA to NFA: eliminating ε-transitions
overview: Remove ε-transitions by following closure → symbol → closure. Recreate the lecture’s A/B/C worked example, update its final states correctly, and check a separate practice variation.
objectives: Apply closure around a consumed symbol using one stated convention.
Preserve acceptance by marking states whose closure intersects the original finals.
Check converted transitions and compare short-string behavior.

keyTerms.definition: A state change that consumes no input symbol.
q plus every state reachable from q through zero or more ε-edges.
An automaton whose state and input may permit zero, one, or several next states.
An NFA that also permits ε-transitions.
The converted state q is final exactly when E(q) intersects the original final set, under the chosen closure construction.

segments.title: Locate ε-NFA among finite-state machines
notes: The opening hierarchy distinguishes finite automata used for recognition from machines with explicit output, then separates DFA, NFA and ε-NFA.
The conversion in this lesson removes ε-transitions while preserving the accepted language. It does not require the result to be deterministic.
segments.speakerNotes: Sa hierarchy, magkakaiba ang DFA, NFA at ε-NFA. Ang gagawin dito ay alisin ang ε-transitions para maging ordinary NFA.
segments.visualDescription: The source shows a finite-state-machine family chart before introducing ε.

segments.title: ε consumes no input symbol
notes: ε denotes the empty word. An ε-edge changes the current state without advancing through an input character.
Do not treat ε as a third alphabet symbol beside0 and 1. It is a transition that consumes zero symbols.
segments.speakerNotes: Ang epsilon ay empty string. Puwedeng lumipat sa state gamit ang epsilon nang walang binabasang input symbol.
segments.visualDescription: The ε slide shows simple graphs and the meaning of the empty string.

segments.title: Compute ε-closure, including the state itself
notes: E(q) contains q and every state reachable from q by zero or more ε-edges. Follow only ε-edges during this step.
The zero-step case matters: q always belongs to E(q), even when no ε-edge leaves it. Use a set so repeated reachable states appear only once.
segments.speakerNotes: Sa closure, isama lagi ang sarili mong state. Sundan lang ang epsilon transitions at huwag ulitin ang kaparehong member ng set.
segments.visualDescription: The source introduces ε-moves and later emphasizes that every closure contains the state itself.

segments.title: Separate conversion from determinization
notes: An ordinary NFA can still have multiple destinations for one symbol. Removing ε-edges is a different task from turning an NFA into a DFA.
We keep the same state names and input alphabet, replace the transition relation, and update accepting states when ε-reachability requires it.
segments.speakerNotes: Ang epsilon-NFA ay gagawing NFA, hindi agad DFA. Puwede pa ring set ang destination sa isang input.
segments.visualDescription: The comparison slide puts an NFA and ε-NFA beside their transition mappings.

segments.title: Use closure → symbol → closure
notes: For each state q and input x, compute δ′(q,x)=E(⋃{δ(r,x):r∈E(q)}). First find the starting closure, then read exactly one symbol, then close the destinations.
This convention includes ε-moves both before and after the symbol. Repeat it independently for every state and every alphabet symbol.
segments.speakerNotes: Ang proseso ay state, epsilon closure, input, tapos epsilon closure ulit. Gawin ito para sa bawat state at bawat input symbol.
segments.visualDescription: The procedure slide gives way to the worked example and its closure–input–closure flow.

segments.title: Read the source example and prepare its table
notes: The actual example starts at A, has final C, and contains ε-edges A→B→C. A loops on 0, B loops on 1, and C loops on both 0 and 1.
Therefore E(A)={A,B,C}, E(B)={B,C}, and E(C)={C}. Begin a new table with rows A,B,C and columns 0,1.
segments.speakerNotes: Sa source example, A ang initial state at C ang final. May epsilon mula A sa B at mula B sa C. Ihanda ang rows na A,B,C at columns na0 at 1.
segments.visualDescription: The blue source graph is shown beside the closure rule; the blank NFA table is introduced around 22:50.

segments.title: Fill A’s two converted transitions
notes: For A on 0: start from {A,B,C}; the 0-moves yield {A}∪∅∪{C}={A,C}; closing those destinations gives {A,B,C}.
For A on 1: the 1-moves from the starting closure yield ∅∪{B}∪{C}={B,C}; their closure is still {B,C}.
segments.speakerNotes: Unahin ang closure ng A: A,B,C. Sa0, A at C ang may moves; pagkatapos ng closure, A,B,C ang sagot. Sa1, B at C ang destinations.
segments.visualDescription: The instructor expands closure sets and symbol destinations while completing A’s row.

segments.title: Finish the B and C rows
notes: B starts from E(B)={B,C}. On0 only C contributes, giving {C}; on 1 the destinations are {B,C}.
C has no outgoing ε-edge, so its closure is just itself and both symbols return to {C}.
The completed table is A:[{A,B,C},{B,C}], B:[{C},{B,C}], C:[{C},{C}].
segments.speakerNotes: Ulitin ang proseso kay B at C. Para kay B,0 ay C at 1 ay B,C. Para kay C, pareho lang na C ang destination sa0 at 1.
segments.visualDescription: The remaining table cells are calculated before the lesson decides which rows are accepting.

segments.title: Update accepting states: A, B, and C all accept
notes: Mark q accepting when E(q) intersects the original final set {C}. A and B can both reach C using only ε; C is already final. The converted accepting set is therefore {A,B,C}.
This preserves empty-word acceptance: the original start A can reach final C without consuming input, so converted start A must be accepting.
segments.speakerNotes: A at B ay makakarating sa original final C gamit lang ang epsilon. Kaya sa converted NFA, final na silang tatlo: A,B,C.
segments.visualDescription: The table gains accepting markers beside all three state rows.

segments.title: Draw the new NFA and combine repeated edges
notes: Every destination in a table cell needs a corresponding edge. For A on 0, the destinations are A,B,C; for A on 1 they are B,C.
When0 and 1 share the same source and target, combine their labels on one arrow. This cleans the drawing without changing the transition relation.
The source’s C-loop label briefly reads1,1; the narration corrects it to0,1 and the table confirms both inputs return to C.
segments.speakerNotes: Iguhit ang lahat ng destinations sa table. Kapag pareho ang source at target ng arrows, puwedeng pagsamahin ang labels na0 at 1 para mas malinaw ang diagram.
segments.visualDescription: The source draws the three final-state nodes, adds edges, then simplifies repeated arrows.
segments.caution: Editorial clarification: the recreated C loop is labeled0,1, following the table and the spoken correction rather than the duplicated label visible in one source frame.

segments.title: Practice variation: a shorter ε-NFA
notes: This is a newly authored exercise, not the video’s machine. Start p0 has ε→p1; p1 has an a-loop and b→final p2.
Its closure sets are E(p0)={p0,p1}, E(p1)={p1}, E(p2)={p2}. The converted p0 acquires p1’s a and b transitions, but p0 is not accepting because its closure does not contain p2.
segments.speakerNotes: Dagdag na practice variation ito, hindi sinabi o iginuhit na example sa video. I-apply ang parehong closure–input–closure procedure.
segments.visualDescription: Original practice figure derived from the method, with a source link back to its explanation.

recap: Compute each epsilon closure, then follow each alphabet symbol from every state in that closure and close destinations.
Make q accepting when E(q) intersects the original final set; this preserves empty-word acceptance.
commonMistakes: Treating ε as an input symbol.
Forgetting the state itself in its epsilon closure.
Following a symbol from q alone and ignoring other closure members.
Using a different closure convention without changing the formula.
Keeping only the old final states instead of closure-intersection finals.
Assuming every NFA transition must have one destination.

questions.prompt: In the source ε-NFA, what is E(A)?
questions.explanation: A reaches itself with zero ε-moves, then B and C using the two ε-edges.

questions.prompt: In the source example, what is δ′(A,0) after closure →0→closure?
questions.explanation: The0-moves from E(A) yield {A,C}; closing A adds B and C, giving {A,B,C}.

questions.prompt: In the source example, what is δ′(A,1)?
questions.explanation: Only B and C in E(A) have1-moves; their closures remain {B,C}.

questions.prompt: Which states are accepting in the source’s converted NFA?
questions.explanation: Each state’s ε-closure contains original final C, so all three must accept.

questions.prompt: Suppose a different ε-NFA has start r and ε-edge r→f, where f is final. Is empty input accepted?
choices: No; one symbol must be consumed
Only if f loops on ε
Yes, because ε reaches f without consuming input
questions.explanation: The run can reach final f while consuming zero input symbols.

questions.prompt: Which statement about E(q) is correct?
choices: It excludes q unless q has an ε-loop
It includes states reached by any alphabet symbol
It includes q via zero ε-moves
questions.explanation: Zero ε-moves are allowed, so q belongs to its own epsilon closure.

questions.prompt: Why close destinations after following a symbol under the chosen convention?
choices: To include states reachable by further ε-moves after that consumed symbol
To remove the symbol from the alphabet
To force the destination to be final
questions.explanation: The target set must include all ε-reachable states after consuming a.

questions.prompt: Which converted diagram is valid for the practice graph?
questions.explanation: Closure of p0 supplies p1’s symbol edges, but the converted diagram labels them a and b; no ε edge remains.

questions.prompt: What is δ′(B,0) in the source conversion?
questions.explanation: E(B)={B,C}; only C has a 0-edge, and E(C)={C}.

questions.prompt: What should happen to a missing symbol destination from a state in an NFA?
choices: Invent a destination at the start
Keep the result empty; do not add an unsupported edge
questions.explanation: An empty transition set is valid for an NFA; conversion does not invent edges.

questions.prompt: A state q has ε-closure {q,f}, with f original-final. How is q treated after conversion?
choices: Nonfinal because q is not f
Final because its closure intersects the final set
Final only when every closure member is final
questions.explanation: E(q)∩F is nonempty, so q must be accepting in the ε-free NFA.

questions.prompt: Why must converted start A accept ε in the source example?
choices: The original A can reach final C using only ε-moves
Every start state must be final
questions.explanation: A→εB→εC consumes no input, so the original accepts ε. Equivalence requires the converted start to accept too.

questions.prompt: For the converted practice NFA, what is the transition from p2 on a?
questions.explanation: The original p2 has no symbol transitions and E(p2)={p2}, so the resulting set is empty.

questions.prompt: Which diagram property confirms ε-elimination succeeded?
choices: Every state has one outgoing edge
questions.explanation: The target machine uses only input-alphabet labels; NFA branching can remain.

questions.prompt: Which trace describes input “ab” from p0 in the practice source?
choices: ε to p1, a-loop at p1, then b to final p2
a to p0, then b to p1
b to p2, then a to p2
ε to p2, then b to p0
questions.explanation: Take the free move to p1, consume a on its loop, and consume b to final p2.
